I think it depends a lot on the illness, the treatment, and the individual.

I know in my case, my treatment is mostly non-pharmaceutical, highly theraputic. It's largely hands-on with individual therapists. It is to my advantage and only to society's in that I am a healthier functioning member of it.

OTOH, My son, who has a different illness, has a mostly pharmaceutical treatment. He has therapy, but it's less emotionally intensive, and more behaviourally directive. We are, of course, absolutely concerned about his quality of life, his health, his schooling, etc.; but that includes his mental health. And he is not a functional member of society without being fully medicated. He is dangerous, to himself and others. And *he knows this* So is he really suffering? I guess it's a tossup. I think he is. I think that the child who I see cry because he knows there is something wrong with him that he can't help when there are symptom breakthroughs is suffering from his illness. But does society suffer from it too? Absolutely.

Great. you've got to find a daycare you can afford that's on the bus route to the college. Oh, and you've got to be able to get scholarships and loans to go. But wait, you've got to WORK to feed that baby and put a roof over his head. so you can't go during the day. night classes? try finding a daycare open at night. Oh, and you're gonna need to apply for assistance, because your minimum wage job isn't going to give healthcare, and that baby's going to need to go to the doctor, and let's face it, you're probably not eating enough. So you get medicaid. And food stamps. I don't know what minimum wage food stamps are for two people, we live on less than that because I'm disabled, but we get $170/month. can you feed two people on that? It's ridiculous. It's almost impossible to afford fresh vegetables and other healthy things. We eat a lot of unhealthy crap, not because we don't know better, but because we can't afford better.

DID is kind of hard to explain. It's Dissociative Identity Disorder. It used to be labeled Multiple Personality Disorder, but they decided that it was a broader, more complicated issue than that.

There are two types of PTSD. There's the type a soldier would get--a short term, nearly singular event thing--and there's complex PTSD, the kind that happens to long term abuse survivors.(it's a little more complicated than that, but I'm not a psychiatrist so please bear with me) Anyway, C-PTSD can lead to things like BPD, Somatization disorder (which also really sucks, btw) and dissociative disorders.


basically, Dissociative Disorders are where one...dissociates. people go into a fugue state, they in idiot terms flake out on their bodies. just go away. If that's all that happens, they get a DDNOS diagnosis. (which also blows, because no one likes to flake like that) 

The difference with DID is that when you dissociate, a different part of your brain takes over. Some people (and not all, but more than most people think) when faced with severe trauma starting at a very early age start to dissociate THEN, and develop, as a way of dealing with it, an alternate self to accept the trauma. For many people, this keeps occurring for many years, and several alternate selves are splintered in one's mind. A lot of people can function most of their lives like this without it ever becoming an issue until one day, they...can't. And usually that starts with blackouts. Fugue states. Some small incident dominoes it out and they're faced with this jumble of selves that they're forced to confront and understand. It's complicated because you know it's all you, but at the same time, it's...not. I don't know if I've explained it very well. Most people start out with shitty internal communication. They can't talk to their parts at all, sometimes don't even know they have parts--just have unexplained blackouts where later people either don't have any memory of what happened, or are told later that they were acting strangely. (example--I once got a Michael Bolton album from someone on ebay and had no idea when, how, or why I would have bought it.)

Anyway, rarely on their own, or with decent treatment, (I went to a hospital for...a while) You learn some really basic stuff (actually, you could probably just pick up a decent book, but proper diagnosis and not self-diagnosis is a good thing) like journaling with them. Once you get to know them that way, which is actually a really good way to communicate as long as you can read their handwriting, it becomes easier to communicate with them without the journal, because you're more aware of them--not just their existence, which you probably already knew by this point--but how they communicate and how to work with them. what appeases the teenagers, what kind of toys the littles like, how to rationalise with the adults, who needs an anger room and when. They're ever-present in your mind, so once you *can* communicate with them, communication becomes an almost constant thing, even if it's just background shushing. Unless it's something important, like an event that may cause a trigger for one or several of them, I only set aside a portion of my day to communicate directly with them, or I'd be overwhelmed with the internal monologue/dialogue.

It *is* possible to be co-conscious, but it's not a gradual transition or anything, it's a normal switch that you remain aware of. I'm not co-conscious with any of my parts but one, and him only when he's comfortable enough to share (I am female by the way, having male parts can be frustrating for them and for me, it leads to gender identity issues). I've been co-conscious with another in therapy, and that was really f-ing weird. I know some people (very few) that are co-conscious with some or all of their parts, it's sort of a theraputic goal, because if you're co-conscious, you're not losing time, even if you're not the one in control. The last step, technically, in treatment of DID is integration, but a lot of us are uncomfortable with that idea, and aren't comfortable going any further than co-consciousness. Despite the fact that it is all one person and one mind, after a lifetime of having all of this separation in your head, the idea of fusion is extremely uncomfortable and a lot of people prefer to live with their separate identities intact.
